awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Task Performance and Causal Claims: Leveraging Network Analysis and Large Language Models to Extract Information from Organizational Hazard Texts
awd_abstract_narration:
Crises – particularly those rising to the level of disasters –demand an organized response. In complex systems of organizational disaster response, core tasks such as communication and coordination of activities become large-scale challenges. This study evaluates such challenges in two research thrusts. The first thrust examines the broader discourse created by official online communications disseminated to the public during the COVID-19 pandemic. The second thrust examines the extent to which an organization's task performance impacts effective collaborations in an emergent multi-organizational disaster response network, with a specific case study of the 2005 Hurricane Katrina. The “lessons learned" from our communications studies are used to synthesize concrete organizational communication strategies that can help practitioners and officials better engage stakeholders, thereby building the trust between the public and officials that is critical for disaster management. The results of our collaboration study inform organizational training efforts for hazard events, which may decrease the friction of collaboration and coordination efforts in response to large-scale disasters and thus contribute to the protection of lives and property.

This study aims to provide insights at multiple levels of the organizational response process, from shared task performance among organizations to the broader structure of public-facing discourse around health hazards and the emergence of multi-organizational response networks. This study leverages the strengths of machine learning-based natural language processing methodologies and network analysis techniques to extract from, and analyze massive corpuses of hazards communications. Thus, this study contributes to methodologies of large-scale information extraction, decreasing costs previously associated with obtaining high-quality data from records while increasing the potential value of underutilized historical case studies.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Introduction: Communication occupies a central role in crisis response.  On the one hand, public-facing organizations are tasked with informing, alerting, and guiding the public as the threat evolves; on the other, all organizations (public-facing or otherwise) must communicate within and among themselves to coordinate activities and maintain situational awareness.  Records of such communications provide a rich source of insights into how responding organizations operate, reflecting communication strategies of authoring organizations as well as providing accounts of activities. However, reliable extraction of high-quality information (e.g. who did what, where, how, with whom, and why) from such records has traditionally proven costly, requiring trained human coders to manually code through large sets of heterogeneous documents. In the work for this doctoral thesis, we leveraged recent advances in machine-learning based natural language processing (ML-NLP) along with network analysis techniques to extract and analyze complex, semantic information from text-based communication records written by organizations responding to hazards and disasters. In particular, we developed methodologies for two distinct case studies: the extraction of causal narratives by officials communicating in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, and organizational task performance in the response to the 2005 Hurricane Katrina disaster.

Intellectual Merits: This research has helped to expand our understanding of how to adapt ML-NLP models, particularly large language models (LLMs), for accurately extracting information on organizational behaviors from massive collections of communication records. We find that breaking extraction workflows into multiple stages of evaluations by LLMs greatly increases model accuracy compared to manual coding efforts by humans. For task performance extraction, we find that incorporating the National Response Framework developed by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security into the LLM workflow provides a well-informed ontology for systematically categorizing task performance.

Our work in extracting and analyzing task performance data on organizations responding to the 2005 Hurricane Katrina paired with previously-coded network data on organizational collaborations gives nuanced insights into how an organization’s work impacts their collaborations made with other organizations. Organizational task performance is found to be related to an organization’s connectivity both locally and globally to the broader collaboration network; however, connectivity will vary based on the nature of the task performed. Although organizations reported to have many collaborations perform larger numbers of tasks, isolated organizations are found to be quite active in task performance as well. Furthermore, working on related tasks is found to be positively associated with collaborative relationships.

Broader Impacts: The methodological development of ML-NLP workflows for extracting complex, semantic features across heterogeneous communications produced during the disaster management cycle sets a framework for future efforts to extract high-quality information on organizational activities accurately and quickly – in nearly a fraction of the time spent by a team of human coders with comparable results.

The work from this project has resulted in a journal publication and continued work toward an article under revision for resubmission to an academic journal. Furthermore, work from this project has been shared at multiple national and international conferences. This project has provided interdisciplinary training and resources to a doctoral candidate, ultimately culminating in the successful completion of a doctoral thesis and PhD degree.
